items.title: I never got to comment on Nvidia-HF because I was OOO, but something that struck me is how HuggingFa...
items.content:
I never got to comment on Nvidia-HF because I was OOO, but something that struck me is how HuggingFace is a steal for Nvidia. HuggingFace's core ability is understanding how to influence the discussion and direction of AI, relative to their resources.

For Nvidia, who is so rich and powerful, this ability is worth easily the ~$10B they paid, but every year. There are many sources of capital other than just hard cash -- HuggingFace is rich in those sources of soft power. It'll be a challenge for Nvidia to keep that culture and to foster it, but that challenge will be valuable growth for the company.

Nvidia is a better buyer than one of the three clouds, as the clouds would feel more pressure to make money on it, to compete directly with github, etc. HuggingFace should now be given the directive of Jensens ambition, to be free from having to think of themselves as a "functioning business unit" and to be the most powerful comm's army in the AI discourse of all time. 

HuggingFace should be free to win the hearts and minds of the next 100 million AI developers, and I'm excited to see it happen. Having worked at HuggingFace, and stared down the barrel of making the company work as an independent public entity, this outcome should've been seen as somewhat inevitable.

Congrats again to @Thom_Wolf @julien_c, @ClementDelangue, and all my friends at @huggingface for making something with such incredible value. Much of the culture was about creating value for the whole community, rather than capturing it for HuggingFace. This is now in line with Nvidia's "all-in" bet on open models (so intelligence isn't monopolized), and this next part of the chapter will be fun.

My first day of work at HuggingFace, fresh off a red eye in Paris, still feels like yesterday (2022). When I posted the prediction below, last year, I actually got hate for it. lol.

✨ I replaced all these SaaS with my own vibe coded now, so about $25,000/mo savings:

- Weather API ...
items.content:
✨ I replaced all these SaaS with my own vibe coded now, so about $25,000/mo savings:

- Weather API -> My own vibe coded weather service using Norway's meteorology API
- Image resizing API -> My own vibe coded image resizing API with NodeJS's Sharp + Redis (saves ~$1,500/mo)
- Google Vision NSFW detection -> My own $0/mo vibe coded NSFW detection service with Python's NudeNET (saves ~$2,500/mo)
- Cloudflare Streaming -> My own $0/mo Nginx VPS video streaming (saves ~$250/mo)
- API Flash -> My own $0/mo screenshot service (for social images) (saves ~$250/mo)
- New Relic + IPHub -> My own $0/mo error monitoring, DDOS blocking and fleet management service (called error2telegram) (saves ~$250/mo)
- Human moderators -> My own moderation on all my sites with @xAI (saves ~$10,000/mo)
- IFTTT -> Telegram bot (saves ~$100/mo)
- Photopea as editor inside Photo AI -> Vibe coded my own photo editor (saves ~$100/mo)
- Mapbox -> Vibecoded my own free replacement with OpenFreeMaps (saves ~$500/mo)
- Uptimerobot -> My own $5/mo Uptime Canary app running on Kuma (saves ~$50/mo)
- Ghost blog -> My own $0/mo blog platform
- Customer support -> @featurebasehq + AI support bot (saves $5,000/mo)
- Scrapingbee/SerpAPI -> My own $1/mo scraper with Patchright (save ~$250/mo)

I think I have reached my final limit of replacing my SaaS services as I have these left, but that'd mean becoming an ICANN registrar (I don't want 😁), managing my own email (I don't want), managing my own hard drives at home in a storage (I don't want) and managing my own servers at home too (I don't want) and running my own GPU rig at home (I don't want):

- Cloudflare Domains
- Cloudflare Email Sending
- Cloudflare R2 Storage
- Backblaze B2 for backups
- Hetzner for all my servers for all my sites (VPS)
- xAI for all LLMs for all my sites (so many things like moderation, writing emails, anything)

items.title: The economic model breaks jobs down into bundles of tasks. AI can help someone complete a task faste...
items.content:
The economic model breaks jobs down into bundles of tasks. AI can help someone complete a task faster or better, do the task itself, leave the task untouched, or create new tasks. 

Based on how you expect AI to affect tasks by 2030, our scenario explorer models AI’s potential impact on the US economy.

The scenario explorer focuses on three possible scenarios: modest, substantial, and extreme. The economy grows across all three scenarios. But in more transformative scenarios, AI automates more knowledge work, so the challenge is making sure that the gains are shared across society.

Like all economic models, ours simplifies a more complex reality. But by building better scenarios of our possible economic future, we can take steps to make sure everyone benefits from it.

items.title: ✨ Okay with lots of help from @javilopen and his Spanish scraping friends I've managed to vibe code ...
items.content:
✨ Okay with lots of help from @javilopen and his Spanish scraping friends I've managed to vibe code my own @Scrapingbee alternative and replace my $249/mo Scrapingbee plan with my own $1/mo scraper running on my VPS!

First I tried OpenSERP, an open source project that seems freshly maintained but it didn't work on my VPS IP or laptop IP and got blocked fast

Then I tried to use residential IP proxies from IPRoyal but they were already quite tainted IPs meaning Google already knew they were scrapers and just blocked about 60% of them already, not so great, also didn't work!

Then I discovered OpenSERP uses a vanilla headless Chrome, Google instantly detects that and blocks that, so literally the entire repo is useless cause it won't even work? I don't get why they don't say that in the docs? OpenSERP is even worse than just basic CURL, as my AI said: "plain curl got 7% blocked but OpenSERP's headless browser got 100% blocked"

So then I just built my own with Playwright and a real Google Chrome on my VPS, headful and persistent context, and slow pacing like every 30 seconds or so

And I got some better residential IP recommendations (which I can't tell you because thenhey t stop working!)

Now I'm at about 90% success rate, which is similar or better than Scrapingbee

And it costs me ~$1/mo (measured by GBs, obviously for text scraping I barely use a lot) instead of the $249/mo I paid Scrapingbee!

My only remaining SaaS now are:
- Cloudflare Domains
- Cloudflare Email Sending
- Cloudflare R2 Storage
- Backblaze B2 for backups
- Hetzner for all my servers for all my sites (VPS)
- xAI for all LLMs for all my sites (so many things like moderation, writing emails, anything)

items.title: friends are regularly surprised when i say i don’t think math is (yet) “solved,” so in the wake of t...
items.content:
friends are regularly surprised when i say i don’t think math is (yet) “solved,” so in the wake of the ns result i figured i’d explain this take a bit more widely.

first, this is massively impressive and clearly an example of AI being, in some respects, far more powerful than the human mind. the team deserves huge praise for attempting and succeeding at this. i’d love to read a technical report on the project (one can always hope :)

but second, here again we ended up with a counterexample rather than a full proof: option C won the NS problem by proving the conjecture false (which was one valid way to solve the problem for sure)

notice a pattern in many of the recent frontier results in ai for math? a striking number involve counterexamples or finding a needle in a haystack.

now don’t get me wrong: this is extraordinarily hard and commendable. but it is only one aspect of mathematicians’ work.

Math is also about:
- finding deep, general mathematical understanding and explanations within proofs
- revisiting proven results to find more « elegant » proofs
- proposing new conjectures and hypotheses that might open « fruitful » directions
- taking the leap of faith of proposing entirely new, « exciting » research programs that may take decades to bear fruit

you may say these are simply further increments on the same intelligence scale, and perhaps point 2 above is already within the reach of current models. possibly

but you could also see this string of results as an extraordinarily powerful, massively parallel extension of search: explore the haystack, find the needle i.e. the counterexample that breaks the conjecture.

that would already be remarkable. but it would still leave open whether models understand the words I emphasized above: « elegant », « fruitful », « exciting ».

as tristan put it in his brief report: “the first llm generated proof levent sent me was the most horrendous i have ever read.”

despite their formidable technical abilities, models still seem to lack something mathematicians rely on constantly: a type of mathematical taste. the ability to distinguish a beautiful argument from a merely valid one, a fertile idea from a sterile one.

i’d be very curious to ask gpt or claude what they think of the result they just proved. do they find it elegant? if they ignore all the human noise about it on the web and history of math, do they appreciate the result and the path to it more than other proofs?

my suspicion is that, outside of the human knowledge that this is an important millennium prize problem, it may not 100% register it as fundamentally different from thousands of other proofs.

or, more intriguingly, perhaps the beauty they find in mathematics is actually alien to our own sense of mathematical beauty, some « horrendous » proof to us might be deeply satisfying to them…

all this to say that we might have significant progress to make in ai for math before declaring the field “solved,” (as too many are posting).

in the meantime, ai will be an extraordinary collaborator for mathematicians. i just hope access to these tools be as widely shared as possible (so that you don’t need a Leven or Sebastien working in a big lab to help you), and that companies stop using mathematics primarily as a demonstration of prowess in their private race.

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: OpenAI's newest board member says we could lose control of AI in the very near ...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: OpenAI's newest board member says we could lose control of AI in the very near term.

• Paul Christiano joins the Foundation Board and its Safety and Security Committee, plus a non-voting seat on the for-profit board
• He led alignment research at OpenAI from 2017 to 2021 and co-created RLHF, then founded the Alignment Research Center
• From his statement: "Based on the recent trajectory of capabilities and the continued difficulty of alignment, I now believe there is a meaningful risk that rapid acceleration in AI capabilities leads to catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term"
• "I do not think that the AI industry in general, including OpenAI, is currently on track to reduce this risk to an acceptable level"
• Full automation of AI R&D could be several months away. Within six months of that, he expects more algorithmic progress than since the transformer

@theojaffee: "There's a word for this. Preference cascade. The situation where people's private opinions reach a tipping point and become publicly expressed and accepted. That is what we're seeing right now with AI safety."

- what gets measured afterward

items.title: Gamow Labs founder @danielmckinn0n reveals how o3 diagnosed the rare genetic disease that killed his...
items.content:
Gamow Labs founder @danielmckinn0n reveals how o3 diagnosed the rare genetic disease that killed his son after a leading neonatal genome lab missed it:

"Our origin story is pretty sad, but unfortunately, it's not unique. Five years ago, I lost my first son to a rare genetic disease. When we say rare disease, we're not talking about rare disease in aggregate. When you add up all of these, we're losing a tremendous number of children to rare diseases that could be diagnosed if our tools were better."

"Two weeks in the NICU we realized something was seriously wrong. The staff ordered a whole genome test, gold standard diagnostic. It came back negative."

"At eight weeks old, we made the impossible decision to withdraw care. Months of diagnostic odyssey, we found the diagnosis for his condition. We also found out it was inherited, which impacted our ability to start a family."

"We tragically had a second loss very late for genetic reasons. My now healthy one-year-old son, Warren, was 16 weeks in utero. Another whole genome sequence came back also negative."

"My whole background is in AI. I called all the labs and requested all the raw data under my HIPAA rights. I wrote what we'd call an agentic loop, pre-Codex, pre-Claude Code. I put o3 in a harness and said, figure this out."

"My jaw hit the ground when I saw that it diagnosed my first son, Owen, that the best neonatal whole genome lab missed a few years ago. At that point I knew I wanted to dedicate my life to solving this problem."
@GamowLabs @OpenAI

items.title:
Warner Music Group went from a legal fight with Suno to helping develop its new AI music models.

Th...
items.content:
Warner Music Group went from a legal fight with Suno to helping develop its new AI music models.

The two settled in November 2025. Today, Suno launched v6 with Warner, BMG and Believe as development partners.

Some new abilities with the v6 models: 

- Rewrite a single lyric or change a chorus without replacing the rest of the song

- Take vocals from one of their songs and drums from another, then combine them

- Pull out specific elements of a song and build around around them

- Use text, audio, images or video as the starting references for music

The three new versions: flagship v6 for precision and control, v6-wild for more experimental results, and a v6-mini free tier. The first two require Pro ($8/mo) or Premier ($24/mo) subscriptions.

Suno also said it is developing artist-specific experiences where artists can choose whether to participate and get paid if they do.

Here’s a thought experiment.

I’m going to ask you to do something evil, one that would make you worse than Hitler and Stalin, and I want to know how much I would have to pay you to be that evil.

I am going to ask to roll a ten-sided die. 

If it comes up zero, every human on the planet will perish. 

If it comes up anything else, I will make you rich.

How much do I have to pay you to get you to play? 

Will you do it for a million dollars? a billion? a trillion?

Do you just not give a fuck about humanity?

In my opinion the only correct answer is from the film Wargames.

 “The only way to win is not to play.”

items.title: Yesterday, Anthropic's alignment science lead put a >10% chance on AI killing all humans within a de...
items.content:
Yesterday, Anthropic's alignment science lead put a >10% chance on AI killing all humans within a decade.

For some lighter reading, Anthropic's economics team just published what happens to the U.S. economy if it doesn't.

Three scenarios for 2030, GDP measured against a world without AI:

- Modest: AI's impact is "something like the internet's." GDP +1.6%.

- Substantial: AI can do half of all knowledge work, most of it on its own. GDP +8.3%. Knowledge-worker wages "essentially flat."

- Extreme: AI does nearly all knowledge work. GDP +32.4% (!) to $44.4T, growth hits 15% a year, and the economy doubles every 4.5 years.

items.title: FrogNano demonstrates that a compact 4-billion-parameter model can reach strong repository-level cod...
items.content:
FrogNano demonstrates that a compact 4-billion-parameter model can reach strong repository-level coding performance through reinforcement learning on synthetic tasks alone, without distillation from larger models. The work addresses the high cost and deployment barriers of frontier SWE agents by testing whether a small model can become a practical coding agent when equipped with the right training loop.

The authors developed an iterative pipeline centered on TaskPilot, an online task-synthesis system that generates and refines executable software-engineering tasks from real repository snapshots, calibrating difficulty to the current policy’s learnability frontier. They paired this with a lightweight harness called Leaf that uses five typed tools and a simple termination rule, then trained the base Qwen3.5-4B model with group-relative DPPO over five successive rounds of task synthesis and RL, for a total of roughly 1,500 synthetic tasks.

Read the paper with an AI tutor: https://t.co/dYAksOJrbB

"It's not like these people have abacuses, but the reads come in and they'll use various different pieces of software to do various different parts of that pipeline."

"At the end, they come up with a packet, and this packet might contain 100, it might contain 10, it might contain one, it might contain zero different variants."

"It was the classic human-driven deep research project, but it's verifiable."

"AI models suck at writing 'cause no one knows what good writing is. This is definitely causative, and here's a very structured line of reasoning to get there."

"It's a perfect task for AI, and the models are getting quite good at it, and I think how we leverage the models is the best in the world."
@GamowLabs

items.title: Pretraining large language models requires enormous compute, yet standard practice has largely aband...
items.content:
Pretraining large language models requires enormous compute, yet standard practice has largely abandoned layer dropout despite its historical success in enabling faster training and inference flexibility. Earlier work showed that randomly skipping entire transformer blocks during training can cut FLOPs while building robustness to reduced-depth execution, but reports of accuracy loss at scale left the technique sidelined in modern recipes.

This study set out to determine whether layer dropout can be configured to match or beat dense baselines in large-scale LLM pretraining while delivering measurable savings in training compute and inference latency. Researchers conducted more than 2400 controlled experiments on decoder-only transformers ranging from 271 million to 8.2 billion parameters, training on datasets up to 160 billion tokens using Cerebras CS-3 systems. They jointly optimized learning rate, weight decay, layer-wise dropout distributions, and temporal schedules, then measured both validation loss and downstream performance under fixed token budgets.

Read the paper with an AI tutor: https://t.co/qpCx2wtXRT

items.title:
There are three types of advice investors can give you: business, investor market, and personal

Mos...
items.content:
There are three types of advice investors can give you: business, investor market, and personal

Most investors are decent at the first two.  They’ve seen a lot of companies and they obviously know what’s attractive to the market

Both skills come from pattern-matching and running in the right circles - basically spreading your time.  Both are also losing value.  AI is rewriting basically everything so patterns are less relevant, and everyone is in the same companies with the same information

The third kind of advice requires the opposite - spending an extreme amount of time understanding the founders and tailoring your advice to what they’re uniquely good and bad at

I’d argue this type of advice matters the most.  If founders have an outsized impact on their companies, and founders differ from each other far more than companies do, then advice tailored to the individual should have an outsized effect on outcomes

This is what @krisfredrickson  is best at.

@gabepereyra and I first met Kris in late 2023 and he invested personally in our series B.  For the past three years, he has helped us:

- hire multiple key folks, because he knew who Gabe and I would work well with
- walk away from what would have been a disastrous acquisition, because he knew we were looking for an easy way out of a harder problem
- translate our pitch for fundraising, because he knew the company inside and out
- keep going when things weren’t working, because he knew what would motivate us

Most importantly, Kris was one of the first to believe in me personally, not just Harvey

Very grateful to continue to partner with him

items.title: Laid off from Meta in May 2023. Coded an entire social platform alone in five months. Launched Janua...
items.content:
Laid off from Meta in May 2023. Coded an entire social platform alone in five months. Launched January 2024. Now 400,000 users.

Perfectly Imperfect founder @tubbytyinthetub on building it before vibe coding existed:

"I got laid off from Meta in May 2023, and I'd had all these neurotic scrambled notes from over the years about how this could be an amazing concept for a social platform."

"When I got laid off, which in some ways was a little bit strategic on my end, I just hit the ground running."

"I spent the next four or five months of my life just coding it all from scratch, and I think you can feel that in the site. There's so many imperfections and bugs."

"A lot of users like that there's a little bit of a janky vibe. You can tell it's not just something someone vibe coded over the weekend."

"We launched in January 2024 after I built the whole app myself, and it's been amazing ever since."
@pi_fyi

items.content:
"You guys solved one of our cases, and this family can confidently have kids now."

Gamow Labs founder @danielmckinn0n on finding what killed a family's son after the world's experts couldn't:

"My son died of a disease called alveolar capillary dysplasia. I'm very close with the lab studying this disease for personal reasons."

"There was one new case that we solved, and they had lost their son a few years ago and never knew why. The world's experts had looked at this case, and we reanalyzed it and we found the molecular cause."

"Our genetic counselor at CCRM, our IVF company, texted my wife and said, 'Oh my God, you guys solved one of our cases, and this family can confidently have kids now.'"

"It was like, this is why we are doing this. The clarity that we gave them about their future and the closure that we gave them about what happened."
@GamowLabs

items.title:
What makes this specific brain map such a massive leap forward?

Our new connectome maps over 166,00...
items.content:
What makes this specific brain map such a massive leap forward?

Our new connectome maps over 166,000 neurons and 125 million connections, and it extends beyond the brain to include the nerve cord, which is analogous to our spinal cord. By comparison, our 2020 hemibrain connectome project with partners, a 3D reconstruction of a portion of the female fruit fly's brain, mapped just 25,000 neurons and 20 million connections.

Plus, having complete maps for both sexes is a game-changer. It finally allows researchers to pinpoint exact structural differences and study how they drive specific biological behaviors.

items.title: I have always assumed that the selfish reason for cloud AI providers to respect our data is competit...
items.content:
I have always assumed that the selfish reason for cloud AI providers to respect our data is competitive: if we find out one of them is untrustworthy while another IS trustworthy, the latter will get our money

(Doesn't work so well for free tiers, though)
items.author: @simonwillison.net
items.summary: Willison argues that cloud AI providers have a competitive, self-interested incentive to respect user data: a provider proven trustworthy over an untrustworthy rival will win customers, though he notes this market mechanism breaks down for free tiers where users pay nothing to switch loyalties.
items.reasoning: Original analytical commentary from a respected AI figure on a persistent and relevant topic (data privacy, provider trust, and market incentives), generating some replies (5) and moderate likes (9). The insight is thoughtful but not breaking news and the argument is fairly familiar to privacy-policy discussions, capping its score.

Why would a studio hire hundreds of people to make a film when AI is cheaper?

Perfectly Imperfect f...
items.content:
Why would a studio hire hundreds of people to make a film when AI is cheaper?

Perfectly Imperfect founder @tubbytyinthetub explains why studios will make AI movies:

"What I'm worried about is movie studios realizing that it costs way less to make a movie using AI. Why would you go through all the bullshit of having to cast a bunch of people and hire hundreds of people to make a film happen?"

"We're gonna go in that direction just because that's where money's gonna lead us. No one's gonna pump the brakes before people in my close family lose their jobs to AI."

"That's gonna happen within the next 10, 15 years, and most people don't even realize it yet."

"Art is more personal to me, and I would hate to see it just become cheaper to prompt an AI movie than to actually have an auteur behind it."
@pi_fyi

items.title: Anthropic's automatic caching billed us $0.022 per turn for the same 8,400 tokens that cost $0.003 o...
items.content:
Anthropic's automatic caching billed us $0.022 per turn for the same 8,400 tokens that cost $0.003 once we placed the cache marker by hand

Automatic caching means one switch, and the system decides what to save. Manual caching means you mark the exact block yourself, so nothing varying ever poisons the entry. That single difference explains the whole gap, and our meter confirmed it across every repeat.

So we wrote down every trick that moved the bill, and each one ships with code you can paste. Every figure below comes from our own runs

> Mark the stable prefix
> Buy minutes, not hours
> Read the usage meter
> Batch the night shift

Then come the two that need explaining. Split planner from executor across two sessions. Cap thinking before it eats its own output.

Our mid-thread model switch billed $0.197 with zero hits. The two-session version read its cache for $0.011, which means the second prefix never charged twice.

Anthropic's docs describe all six features. Our meter readings show what each one actually saves.

The full tutorial walks through every trick with Python and cURL. 
Full breakdown ↓↓

items.content:
I think for Samsung and LG it's a competitive race to the bottom

TVs in Korea are more expensive to produce than in China, but somehow they have to try survive

So their idea (well Samsung started it) was to try make money in other ways, like putting ads in their TVs, then the advertisers asked for better targeting so they needed data, so they started tracking what you watch and listening to what you say at home with the microphone and sending it back to their servers

It's a race to the bottom and this is stuff you actually DO need regulation for to stop it because they're all competing so without regulation this won't stop because people will just buy the cheaper TV I think

1. Choose and shape the ...
items.content:
These are probably the four most important skills for engineers right now:

1. Choose and shape the right model for a task
2. Design evals that reflect how the system would be used
3. Serve a model under latency, cost, and quality constraints
4. Route requests and define policies across the system

These skills are at the heart of what we are now calling "specialized intelligence", and Forge '26 is a great opportunity to learn about them.

Forge '26 is @FireworksAI_HQ's flagship conference for specialized intelligence, and it's just coming up in a couple of months.

Who is the ideal candidate to attend?

• Application builders
• Model builders
• System engineers
• Technical leaders
• Anyone else making AI work in production

What would you get from this?

You'll leave the conference with a bag full of practical ideas you can apply to your own AI systems.

You'll learn how experienced teams choose models, design evals, serve them, and route requests. They'll share what worked, what failed, and how those decisions affected quality, latency, and cost.

Date: November 3
Location: Pier 27 in San Francisco.

You need to submit an application, and if you are selected, you can attend for free.

Use this link to apply:

https://t.co/eRA0hneVv3

Thanks to the Fireworks team for partnering with me on this post.

I'm trying really, really hard not to be cynical and to think these people mean well and want the best for everyone.

But my mind can't square that with the reality of how much money they are making (and stand to make) by working on this supposedly killer technology.

This isn't some sort of alien attack brought upon us. This crisis is of our own creation, fueled by these same people who keep telling us the end is near.

Why don't you stop?

items.title: A short textbook "An elementary introduction to information geometry" by Frank Nielsen (2020) is now...
items.content:
A short textbook "An elementary introduction to information geometry" by Frank Nielsen (2020) is now in the @ChapterPal's collection.

The book provides a foundational entry into the differential geometric study of probability, statistics, and machine learning.

Designed for graduate students, researchers, and practitioners in information sciences, the book assumes a basic working knowledge of linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and classical probability and statistics.

While the text introduces the necessary differential geometry from first principles—covering tangent spaces, metric tensor fields, and affine connections—prior familiarity with basic differential notation helps reader comprehension.

The scope focuses primarily on finite-dimensional parametric families of probability distributions, presenting geometric frameworks to analyze decision-making, estimation, and optimization.

All books on ChapterPal are free to read with a free account,

Read the book with an AI tutor: https://t.co/5ZjnzTURys

The table of contens:

1. Introduction
  - 1.1. Overview of information geometry
  - 1.2. Outline of the survey
  - References
2. Prerequisite: Basics of differential geometry
  - 2.1. Overview of differential geometry: Manifold $(M, g, \nabla)$
  - 2.2. Metric tensor fields $g$
  - 2.3. Affine connections $\nabla$
    * 2.3.1 Covariant derivatives $\nabla_X Y$ of vector fields
    * 2.3.2 Parallel transport $\prod^\nabla_c$ along a smooth curve $c$
    * 2.3.3 $\nabla$-geodesics $\gamma_\nabla$: Autoparallel curves
    * 2.3.4 Curvature and torsion of a manifold
  - 2.4. The fundamental theorem of Riemannian geometry: The Levi-Civita metric connection
  - 2.5. Preview: Information geometry versus Riemannian geometry
  - References
3. Information manifolds
  - 3.1. Overview
  - 3.2. Conjugate connection manifolds: $(M, g, \nabla, \nabla^*)$
  - 3.3. Statistical manifolds: $(M, g, C)$
  - 3.4. A family $\{(M, g, \nabla^{-\alpha}, \nabla^{\alpha}=(\nabla^{-\alpha})^*)\}_{\alpha\in \mathbb{R}}$ of conjugate connection manifolds
  - 3.5. The fundamental theorem of information geometry: $\nabla$ $\kappa$-curved $\Leftrightarrow$ $\nabla^*$ $\kappa$-curved
  - 3.6. Conjugate connections from divergences: $(M, D)\equiv (M, {^{D}}g, {^{D}}\nabla, {^{D}}\nabla^*={^{D^*}}\nabla)$
  - 3.7. Dually flat manifolds (Bregman geometry): $(M, F)\equiv (M, {^{B_F}}g, {^{B_F}}\nabla, {^{B_F}}\nabla^*={^{B_{F^*}}}\nabla)$
  - 3.8. Hessian $\alpha$-geometry: $(M, F, \alpha)\equiv (M, {^{F}}g, {^{F}}\nabla^{-\alpha}, {^{F}}\nabla^\alpha$
  - 3.9. Expected $\alpha$-manifolds of a family of parametric probability distributions: $(\mathcal{P}, {_{\mathcal{P}}}g, {_{\mathcal{P}}}\nabla^{-\alpha}, {_{\mathcal{P}}}\nabla^{\alpha})$
  - 3.10. Criteria for statistical invariance
  - 3.11. Fisher-Rao expected Riemannian manifolds: $(\mathcal{P}, {_{\mathcal{P}}}g)$
  - 3.12. The monotone $\alpha$-embeddings and the metric gauge freedom
  - 3.13. Dually flat spaces and canonical Bregman divergences
  - References
4. Some applications of information geometry
  - 4.1. Natural gradient in Riemannian space
    * 4.1.1 The vanilla gradient descent method
    * 4.1.2 Natural gradient and its connection with the Riemannian gradient
    * 4.1.3 Natural gradient in dually flat spaces: Connections to Bregman mirror descent and ordinary gradient
    * 4.1.4 An application of the natural gradient: Natural Evolution Strategies (NESs)
  - 4.2. Some illustrating applications of dually flat manifolds
  - 4.3. Hypothesis testing in the dually flat exponential family manifold $(\mathcal{E}, \mathrm{KL}^*)$
  - 4.4. Clustering mixtures in the dually flat mixture family manifold $(\mathcal{M}, \mathrm{KL})$
  - References
5. Conclusion: Summary, historical background, and perspectives
  - 5.1. Summary
  - 5.2. A brief historical review of information geometry
  - 5.3. Perspectives
  - References
A. Monte Carlo estimations of $F$-divergences
  - References
B. The multivariate Gaussian family: An exponential family
  - References

items.title: @wittgenfrog @premnsikka Fair concern—but I’d separate ownership of the LLM from ownership of the da...
items.content: @wittgenfrog @premnsikka Fair concern—but I’d separate ownership of the LLM from ownership of the data. A US or Chinese model provider may supply the model, while the data can remain under UK customer control in a UK-hosted, encrypted, access-controlled deployment with contractual no-training terms. The harder strategic issue is dependency: if a vendor becomes the operating layer for the NHS, defence or government, switching costs and institutional lock-in can become material even without that vendor owning the underlying data centres. And all the more a reason for the UK to build more of our own data centres and reintegrate with the EU for example on data residency rules.

Why does the algorithm never serve you the genre you'd love most?

Perfectly Imperfect founder @tubb...
items.content:
Why does the algorithm never serve you the genre you'd love most?

Perfectly Imperfect founder @tubbytyinthetub says it comes down to an ad you might have skipped:

"It's absolutely homogenizing, specifically taste."

"I felt my own taste was becoming algorithmic, and I kind of felt like I was trapped in this space where only four artists existed."

"If you're only listening to EDM music, you're never gonna be served an alt country song from the '90s. Even though that might be your destiny genre."

"Why take the risk? Because you might close the app sooner, and you might not see a certain advertisement. There's no reason to give too much discovery options."

"The best way to teleport out of your bubble is to surround yourself with different types of people. Go IRL, stay for the opener of an artist in your town."
@pi_fyi

items.title: While building ChapterPal, I created a virtually perfect OCR pipeline that supports both articles an...
items.content:
While building ChapterPal, I created a virtually perfect OCR pipeline that supports both articles and textbooks and outputs markdown with illustrations, tables (as complex as the original LaTeX that was used to generate them), and math equations in LaTeX.

I say "virtually" perfect because I'm working alone and I don't have many resources to do a really thorough validation, so I base my conclusion on the results I get when I add to ChapterPal's collection articles or books not having a LaTeX source.

Do you have any challenging scientific paper or book you would like to OCR into markdown? Please use ChapterPal and let me know if you see any conversion artifacts that shouldn't be there or that way.

If you decide to test, you should use the Premium OCR option. If your source PDF has many pages, you might need a paid account. You can use the free 7-day trial to get one. Your card will not be charged if you cancel your trial during the first 7 days.

(I don't have access to your credit card: the card processing goes though @stripe.)

Pluto lost its planet status 20 years ago. Of the three criteria for planethood, Pluto meets the first two qualifications: it orbits the sun and is round. But it fails the third because it hasn’t cleared its celestial “neighborhood,” meaning it is actually a dwarf planet. Yeah, that's a hard astrophysics requirement, not a soft emotional one.

“Plutokiller” Mike Brown explains the ongoing drama:
